text: Is the father's decision not to pay based on a belief that the "kidnapping" call is a scam or that his daughter is not actually in danger?
Is the daughter in genuine danger—i.e., is this a real kidnapping?
Does the father refuse to pay because he physically cannot obtain or deliver one hundred million yen?
Does the father refuse because he believes paying the ransom will not save his daughter (e.g., the kidnapper will kill her anyway)?
Does the father believe that paying the ransom will not save his daughter specifically because the kidnapper will kill the hostage regardless of whether the money is paid?

Does the father believe that attempting to pay the ransom—following the kidnapper's instructions to come alone—would result in his daughter's death (or his own), e.g., because the "come alone" setup will lead to them both being killed?

Would following the "come alone, no police" instruction make the father unable to rescue his daughter—because paying alone means there is no one to help or alert authorities, ensuring the kidnapper can kill them both?
Does the father conclude that, by coming alone as instructed, he himself would be killed by the kidnapper—so that refusing to pay is about saving himself rather than his daughter?

Does the father decide not to pay because the kidnapper's demand that he come alone and not involve the police means there is no way to trace or catch the kidnapper—so paying would not lead to his daughter's safe return?
Does the father refuse to pay as part of a deliberate strategy to save his daughter—for example, to buy time, force the kidnapper to make contact again, or allow police to trace the call?
Is the father's strategy to have the police trace the call—meaning he is (or will be) involving the police despite the "no police" instruction?

Is the father's strategy to force the kidnapper to make contact again—for instance, by refusing so the kidnapper must call back, giving him another chance to learn his daughter's location or to stall?

Is the father buying time so that the kidnapper's deadline ("by noon tomorrow") will pass without payment, and something specific will happen by then to save his daughter (e.g., the kidnapper will be caught, or a rescue is already planned)?
Does the father recognize the kidnapper's voice or something in the call—such that he now understands something about who took his daughter and why?

Does the father refuse because he believes the kidnapper intends to kill his daughter at the moment of the money handover (to eliminate a witness), so refusing payment avoids creating that fatal moment?
Does the father believe that his daughter would be killed once the kidnapper has the money and no longer needs her alive as leverage—meaning payment itself seals her fate?

Does the father believe that, at the handover, the kidnapper will kill both the daughter and him (the father) because the father, having come alone as instructed with the money, would be a witness with no protection?
Does the father believe the kidnapper will kill his daughter at the handover because the father will have seen the kidnapper, making his daughter a witness who must be silenced?

Is the fact that the demand came "over a smartphone" (rather than a landline) important to the father's reasoning—for example, does it reveal the location or the identity/whereabouts of the kidnapper?
Does the father reason that as long as he does not pay, the kidnapper will keep his daughter alive to use her as leverage—whereas once the exchange happens, the kidnapper would kill her as a witness?
Does the father reason that not paying keeps his daughter alive because the kidnapper needs her as leverage?
Does the father know something the kidnapper does not—such that if he paid, the kidnapper would realize this knowledge and kill his daughter, but by refusing he hides it?
Is the father's daughter already dead at the time of the call (or he believes so), making the ransom demand a deception and payment pointless?
Is the father himself the real target—the kidnapper's true aim is to lure the father to come alone in order to kill him, using the daughter as bait?
Does the daughter, in her plea over the smartphone, communicate something to her father—a code, a clue, or a message—that leads him to decide not to pay?
Is the reason the kidnapper would kill the daughter at the handover that she can identify him—i.e., she has seen his face?

Does the father refuse because he realizes that at any handover the kidnapper intends to kill his daughter (since she has seen his face), so the only way to keep her alive is to prevent the handover from ever taking place?

Does the father believe that if he refuses to pay, the kidnapper—still hoping to get the money—will keep his daughter alive rather than kill her, whereas completing the payment would bring about the handover where she'd be killed as a witness?
By refusing to pay, does the father intend to provoke the kidnapper into moving or revealing his daughter—so that her location can be discovered?
Has the father already alerted the police before or during this call (so his refusal is part of a plan already in motion), even though he won't rely on tracing this particular call?
Is there a twist about the family relationship—e.g., is the "kidnapper" someone known to the family (a relative, the mother, or someone the daughter trusts)?
If the father refuses to pay, does he believe his daughter will ultimately survive—that refusing leads to her being freed or rescued?
Is the father's refusal intended to save his daughter's life?
Does the father believe that if he refuses to pay, the kidnapper will eventually give up and release his daughter (because keeping a hostage is not worth it without payment)?
Does the father have an alternative plan to save his daughter that does not involve paying the ransom—such as going to her himself, using non-police help, or some other means?
Does the father's alternative plan rely on the one hundred million yen itself—for example, using the money as bait or in a way other than handing it over as ransom?
Does the father's alternative plan rely on knowing or figuring out where his daughter is being held?
Does the father's alternative plan depend on the kidnapper being someone whose identity or motives the father knows or can determine?

Does the father accept that his daughter will likely die no matter what, and refuse to pay so that the kidnapper gains nothing and so that his daughter is not killed merely as a disposable witness after a payment?

Does the father refuse the ransom *as demanded*—believing that if he does not comply with the "come alone by noon" terms, the kidnapper will be forced to change the deal (e.g., allow a different exchange, or keep her alive longer), giving him a better chance to save her?

Is the father's alternative plan essentially to do nothing but refuse—trusting that the kidnapper, unable to get money, will neither kill his daughter (losing his leverage) nor release her, yet something about the situation will eventually save her?

Is the father's alternative plan to have the kidnapper caught or killed by someone or something other than the police—for example, by the kidnapper's own associates, a rival, or the father's own hired people?

Is the father's central reason for refusing that the ransom payment necessarily leads to a handover—and the kidnapper, needing to silence the daughter who has seen his face, would kill her at that handover?
Would the kidnapper kill the daughter specifically at the handover because that is when he would otherwise release/return her—and releasing her alive would let her identify him to police?

Does the father refuse because he concludes that paying is futile—the kidnapper will kill his daughter at the handover—so paying would only satisfy the kidnapper and cause her death, while refusing at least avoids handing her over to be killed?

Does the father refuse because, knowing the kidnapper will kill his daughter rather than return her at any handover, the only way to preserve any chance of her survival is to never bring about that handover—keeping her alive as an unreleased hostage rather than delivered to her death?

Is it accurate that the father refuses because he realizes payment cannot save his daughter—the kidnapper will kill her at the handover because she has seen his face—so paying would merely be futile, and he chooses not to deliver both the money and his daughter to a killer?
